When someone says a person is "burning the candle at both ends," they mean that person is exhausting themselves by doing too much, resting too little, and living at a pace their body and mind simply cannot sustain. It usually describes someone who stays up very late and wakes up very early, or someone who works extremely hard all day and also fills their evenings with other demanding activities — leaving almost no time to recover.

In short: you are overworking yourself to the point where you are running out of energy, just like a candle that is being used up twice as fast.
The Image Behind the Idiom (Why a Candle?)

To truly understand this idiom, you need to picture a real candle.

A regular candle has one wick at the top. You light it, it burns slowly from the top down, and it lasts a long time. Now imagine someone lights both ends of the candle — the top and the bottom at the same time. Two things immediately happen:

  • The candle burns twice as fast.
  • It goes out much sooner than it normally would.

This is physically wasteful and completely impractical, because the candle destroys itself at double speed and gives you far less total light than it otherwise could have.

Now replace the candle with a person. The wax of the candle represents your energy, health, and time. The two flames represent the two ends of your day — early mornings and late nights. When you push yourself from both ends — sleeping very late and waking very early, or working all day and partying all night — you are consuming your energy at a reckless speed, just like that candle. You are heading toward burnout.
The Origin and History

This idiom is very old. It comes from a French proverb — "brusler la chandelle par les deux bouts" — which literally means "to burn the candle by both ends." The earliest known written record in English appears in Randle Cotgrave's A Dictionarie of the French and English Tongues, published in 1611.

Back in those days, candles were expensive and precious. They were not a luxury — they were the primary source of light in people's homes. Wasting a candle by burning both ends was seen as extremely reckless and foolish. The idiom carried that same sense of foolishness: you are wasting something precious — your own health and energy.

Over the centuries, the phrase crossed into everyday English and has been widely used ever since.
The Famous Poem That Captured This Perfectly

One of the most beautiful expressions of this idiom comes from American poet Edna St. Vincent Millay, who wrote a short poem called "First Fig" in 1920:

My candle burns at both ends;
It will not last the night;
But ah, my foes, and oh, my friends—
It gives a lovely light!

Notice what Millay does here. She admits that burning the candle at both ends is destructive — "It will not last the night." She knows she is wearing herself out. But she also celebrates it — "It gives a lovely light!" She is saying: yes, I am living recklessly and exhausting myself, but I am also living vividly, passionately, and fully.

This poem perfectly captures the double nature of the idiom — the danger and the appeal.
The Two Sides of the Idiom

This idiom carries two different feelings depending on how it is used:

The warning side (more common):
Most of the time, when someone says you are burning the candle at both ends, it is a gentle warning. They are telling you that you are heading toward exhaustion, illness, or breakdown. It is said with concern.

"You've been working 16-hour days for weeks. You're burning the candle at both ends — you need to slow down."

The glamorous/romantic side (less common):
Sometimes, especially in literature or when someone is young and full of energy, the phrase is used with a sense of excitement and defiance. It suggests living life intensely — squeezing every drop of experience out of every day, consequences be damned. Millay's poem is a perfect example of this.
The Tone and Connotation

The idiom is slightly negative in tone. It implies:

  • Poor judgment or a lack of self-care
  • A lifestyle that is unsustainable
  • That the person will eventually collapse or fall sick

It is not a compliment in most situations. It is either a warning from someone who cares about you, or a way of describing someone's situation with worry. However, it is never harsh or rude — it is neutral to sympathetic in feeling.
How to Use It

Structure: The idiom is almost always used in one of these forms:

  • "She is burning the candle at both ends." (describing someone)
  • "He has been burning the candle at both ends." (past continuous — suggests it's been going on for a while)
  • "If you keep burning the candle at both ends, you'll burn out." (as a warning)
  • "I've been burning the candle at both ends lately." (self-reflection)

Register: This is a phrase used in everyday, informal conversation. You can use it with friends, family, or colleagues. It is not overly formal, but it is also not slang — it is perfectly acceptable in most situations, including slightly formal writing.
Example Sentences

Here are several examples showing it used in different contexts:

  1. "Maria is finishing her thesis, working a part-time job, and taking care of her kids. She's really burning the candle at both ends."
  2. "You look exhausted. Have you been burning the candle at both ends again?"
  3. "As a medical student, James was used to burning the candle at both ends — studying until midnight and waking up at 5 AM for rounds."
  4. "My doctor told me I need to stop burning the candle at both ends before my body forces me to stop."
  5. "During fashion week, the designers burn the candle at both ends — up late finishing collections and up early for shows."
What It Does NOT Mean

To avoid confusion, here is what the idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean someone is wasting money.
  • It does not specifically mean someone is lazy (the opposite, in fact).
  • It does not always mean staying up late — more broadly it means overextending oneself in any direction.
  • It is not the same as being stressed. A person can be stressed but still resting. Burning the candle at both ends specifically implies overdoing activity with too little recovery.
Similar Expressions

If you ever want to express the same idea with different words, these expressions carry a similar meaning:

  • "Spreading yourself too thin" — taking on so many commitments that you can't do any of them well.
  • "Running on empty" — continuing to push forward even though you have no energy left.
  • "Working yourself to the bone" — working extremely hard until you are exhausted.
  • "Burnout" — the state of total exhaustion that results from burning the candle at both ends for too long.
The Core Takeaway

This idiom is about the danger of unsustainable living. A candle burned at both ends gives a bright, intense light — but it dies very quickly. A person who pushes themselves from all directions may achieve a lot — but they will eventually crash.

The idiom is a reminder that energy, health, and time are finite resources, just like the wax of a candle. You can spend them wisely, or you can burn through them recklessly. The choice, as always, is yours — but the idiom quietly warns you of the consequences.
